props.title: Devil-May-Care
props.initialSlug: Romantic musical about a dashing French nobleman

sections.content: **Devil-May-Care** (1929) marks a fascinating transition point in early sound cinema, starring Ramon Novarro in his first "talkie" performance. This MGM musical romance arrived at a crucial moment when Hollywood was frantically adapting to sound technology, following the success of **The Jazz Singer** (1927). The film showcases both the ambitions and limitations of early sound musicals, with Novarro performing several operetta-style numbers in both English and French, demonstrating Hollywood's early attempts to maintain international appeal despite language barriers.

sections.content: What makes **Devil-May-Care** particularly noteworthy is its place in the transition from silent romantic leads to sound-era stars. Novarro, like **John Gilbert** in **His Glorious Night** (1929), faced the challenge of adapting his performance style to sound requirements. Unlike Gilbert, whose career famously suffered in the transition, Novarro managed to maintain his appeal, though the film reveals the sometimes awkward staging typical of early sound productions, with actors often positioned unnaturally near hidden microphones. SUBHEAD: Technical Innovation and Musical Integration

The film's technical achievements deserve special attention. Sound engineer Douglas Shearer (who would later win multiple Academy Awards) developed innovative methods to capture both dialogue and musical numbers clearly - no small feat in 1929. The production team's solutions to early sound-recording challenges influenced later musicals like **The Rogue Song** (1930) and **New Moon** (1930), establishing techniques that would become industry standards.
